intro: A teacher writes one sentence on the board, erases it, and writes it again, five times, until it finally argues something. Across the hall a student writes his grandmother's kitchen as a paragraph, then as a poem, and finds that the poem knows something the paragraph did not. Both of them are doing the same thing: taking what is in their heads and shaping it so a stranger can follow it and feel it.

This unit is about the shapes writing can take. First the essay: a thesis that takes a real position, paragraphs that each prove one point, evidence that is introduced and explained instead of dropped, a voice that sounds fair and sure, and the honest work of rewriting. You will also learn the informative shapes, compare and contrast, cause and effect, and definition, and how to write well when a clock is running.

Then the story and the poem: openings that pull, dialogue that sounds like people, pacing that speeds and slows, details from all five senses, a point of view chosen on purpose, and an ending that is earned. You will write a true story and a made-up one, then poems, with attention to line breaks, images and sound, and you will meet the haiku, free verse and the sonnet. At the end, you will read your work aloud and gather it into a class book.
bigQuestion: How does the form you choose, essay, story or poem, change what your writing can say?

timeline.t: Shakespeare's sonnets are printed: 154 poems of fourteen lines each, still the model for the form.
The Declaration of Independence states a claim, lists evidence, and reasons to a conclusion: an argument essay for a nation.
Poe publishes 'The Raven,' a poem built on rhythm, rhyme and repeated sound.
Frederick Douglass publishes his Narrative, a personal story that is also an argument against slavery.
Walt Whitman publishes Leaves of Grass and shows what free verse can do.
Lincoln's Gettysburg Address proves an argument can be short: about 270 words.
Twain lets a boy narrate Huckleberry Finn in his own voice, a lesson in first-person point of view.
A second collection of Emily Dickinson's poems appears, their images and dashes reaching readers she never met.
Carl Sandburg's 'Chicago' turns a city into a person with precise, physical words.
Your class writes essays, stories and poems, reads them aloud, and binds them into an anthology.

words.d: the main claim of an essay, stated in one sentence, that the rest of the essay supports
the sentence that states the single point a body paragraph will prove
the explanation that connects evidence to a claim and shows why the evidence proves it
the strongest objection to a claim, which a careful writer names and answers
a fair, even voice that rests on evidence rather than on the writer's feelings
re-seeing a draft and changing its ideas and structure, not just its surface
the speed at which a story moves, set by sentence length and how much time a passage covers
a detail the reader can see, hear, smell, taste or touch
the position from which a story is told, and how much the narrator knows
the narrator's brief look back at what the events of a story meant
a picture in words that the reader can sense, used in place of an abstract statement
the place where a line of poetry ends, chosen to create a pause or emphasis

test.q: Which sentence is a debatable, specific thesis?
choices: The library should stay open until 8 p.m. because most students cannot get there before dinner.
This essay is about the library.
test.why: It takes a side, gives a reason, and could be argued against. The others state a fact, announce, or ask.

test.q: What are the three parts of a standard introduction, in order?
test.why: The hook draws the reader in, background prepares them, and the thesis comes last.

test.q: A topic sentence contains two reasons joined by 'and also.' What should the writer do?
choices: Split it into two paragraphs, one per reason
test.why: Each body paragraph proves one point. Two reasons need two paragraphs.

test.q: Which of these is a dropped quotation?
choices: According to the coach, 'Practice starts at six.'
The coach said practice starts at six.
'Practice starts at six.' So players should sleep early.
As the schedule shows, practice starts at six.
test.why: The quotation appears with no signal phrase or source, so the reader cannot tell who said it.

test.q: What must follow every piece of evidence in a body paragraph?
choices: Reasoning that explains how it proves the point
test.why: Evidence does not speak for itself. Reasoning connects it to the claim.

test.q: Which sentence keeps an objective tone while still arguing?
choices: The new rule is obviously ridiculous.
Tardies doubled in the month after the new rule began.
Honestly, the rule is the worst.
test.why: It argues through evidence in plain, fair language rather than through feeling words.

test.q: An essay explains the differences between two Chicago neighborhoods, one feature at a time. What is its shape?
test.why: Taking each feature in turn and comparing both subjects under it is the point-by-point shape.

test.q: Which activity is revision rather than editing?
choices: Cutting a paragraph that does not support the thesis
test.why: Revision changes ideas and structure. The others are surface fixes.

test.q: In a timed essay, what should the first five minutes be used for?
choices: Reading the prompt twice and planning a thesis and reasons
test.why: Planning prevents wandering, and there is no second draft to fix it later.

test.q: Which opening drops the reader into a specific moment?
choices: The weather was nice that day.
The ice cream was already on the floor when Dad walked in.
test.why: It shows a moment in progress and raises a question about what happens next.
The comma goes inside the closing quotation mark, followed by a lowercase tag.

test.q: To slow the pacing at the most important moment of a story, a writer should:
choices: Skip the moment in one sentence
Stretch the moment with detail and dialogue
test.why: Slowing down means giving the key moment the most words, as a scene.

test.q: Which sentence uses a sense other than sight?
choices: The hallway was long and gray.
The floor smelled of bleach and wet boots.
test.why: Smell is a sense beyond sight. The other sentences describe only what is seen.

test.q: 'That is why you should always tell the truth.' What is this ending?
test.why: A moral states the lesson directly instead of showing what changed in the narrator.

test.q: Which form is fourteen lines with a set rhyme pattern?
test.why: A sonnet is fourteen lines, usually ten syllables each, with a set rhyme scheme.

write.prompt: Take one memory you wrote about in this unit. Make a claim: which form, prose narrative or poem, told that memory more truly? Support your claim with evidence from your own two drafts and from the chapter, and explain your reasoning.
tips: Claim: name the form and say in one sentence why it served the memory better.
Evidence: quote one line or sentence from each of your drafts and point to a specific tool, such as a line break, a precise verb or a sensory detail.
Reasoning: explain how that tool changed what a reader could see or feel, not just that you liked it.
The other side: admit one thing the other form did better, and answer it.
